tour.title: Plaka, Anafiotika & Monastiraki
tour.summary: From a king's constitution to a sultan's mosque: the old town under the Acropolis — Plaka's lanes, an island village on the slope, and the bazaar where Athens eats and haggles.
tour.overviewText:
Athens arrives first as noise and heat — traffic on Vasilissis Amalias, motorbikes on the pavement, a wall of white concrete blocks poured over something much older. Then you turn off the avenue, the street narrows to the width of a doorway, and the city goes quiet. This walk is about that turn: the old neighbourhoods pressed against the foot of the Acropolis, where Athens has been lived in, without a break, since the Stone Age.

Plaka — the name is old Athenian, first written down in the 1600s, and it probably comes from an Arvanitika word for 'old', though some say it was a marble plaque at a crossroads — is the city's oldest quarter, a knot of lanes on the north and east slopes of the rock. Because nobody ever cleared it away, it carries every layer of the city at once: ancient street lines, a Byzantine church, an Ottoman-era bazaar, and the neoclassical houses built after independence. Anafiotika, the white village clinging to the slope above, was built in the 1830s by workmen from the Cycladic island of Anafi; they came to build a king's palace and stayed, and their quarter still looks like an island that fell into the city.

Religion is never far away. Greece is one of the most Orthodox countries in the world — most people are baptised into the Greek Orthodox Church even if they rarely attend — and the Church of Greece, self-governing since 1833, sits at the centre of national identity, not only of faith. You will stand in front of its cathedral and, a few streets away, at a mosque that became a museum. Politics is here too. Modern Greece was born in a war of independence against the Ottoman Empire that began in 1821 and was recognised by 1830, and the square where this walk starts is named for the constitution a king was forced to grant in 1843. The 20th century brought occupation, civil war and a military dictatorship, and the monarchy was abolished by referendum in 1974. Then, between 2009 and 2018, the debt crisis: three international bailouts, an economy that shrank by more than a quarter, unemployment above a quarter of the workforce, and hundreds of thousands of educated Greeks leaving the country. Supporters of the rescue point to reform and recovery; critics count what was lost. Both are part of the street you are walking.

The route is short and mostly flat, with one steep patch. You begin at Syntagma Square (plateia means square) with the Changing of the Guard, slip into the National Garden and out past the Zappeion, cross to the cathedral, then drop into Plaka's Adrianou Street, climb the Anafiotika lanes, and come down through the Roman Agora to finish in Monastiraki's bazaar. Give it half a day.

Wear shoes with grip — the marble and cobbles are polished by two thousand years of feet — carry water in September's heat, and keep a little cash for the flea market. Then start walking.
tour.difficulty: Easy to moderate. Syntagma, the National Garden and Monastiraki are flat and paved; Plaka is level but its stone lanes are uneven. The one real climb is Anafiotika, a short flight of steep, narrow, stepped lanes with no handrails. Expect polished marble, cobbles and kerbs throughout — wear shoes with grip.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start mid-morning, around 09:30 to 10:00, so the garden is still cool, the ticketed sites are open, and you reach Monastiraki as the evening crowd builds. Sunday is the best single day: the Grand Change of the Guard at 11:00, with the military band, and the real flea market in Avissinia Square in the morning. In early September, start early or late and avoid the midday heat.

stops.name: Syntagma Square & the Changing of the Guard
stops.narration:
Stand on the pavement in front of the Parliament building and look for the two soldiers in white skirts. Those are the Evzones — the ceremonial Presidential Guard, whose name is ancient Greek for 'well-girt', the old word for light infantry — and they are guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, a marble relief of a dying soldier carved into the base of the building. The tomb was added in 1932 to honour the unidentified dead of Greece's wars, and the names of the battles are cut into the stone around it.

The performance is the point. The Evzones stand perfectly still, then move in a slow, exaggerated march, lifting each leg high and bringing it down hard — a style that honours the klephts, the irregular fighters of the independence war. Their uniform is deliberate national theatre: the fustanella, a white kilt made from some thirty metres of cloth with 400 pleats (said to stand for the 400 years of Ottoman rule), a scarlet fez with a long black tassel, and tsarouchia — heavy red leather clogs, about a kilo and a half each, studded with nails and crowned with a black pompom. Every recruit must be at least 1.87 metres tall, and they carry the American M1 Garand rifle, kept on after the war and used only for ceremony.

The change happens every hour, on the hour, and takes a few minutes: two new guards, two old ones, and a corporal to supervise. On Sunday at 11am the whole guard turns out with a military band and marches down from its barracks — that is the version worth timing your morning for. Stand to the side, not straight in front of the guards; a plain-clothes officer will move you if you get in the way, and the guards themselves are forbidden to speak.

Now look past them at the building. This was the Old Royal Palace, finished in the 1840s for King Otto, the Bavarian prince the great powers imposed on newly independent Greece. In September 1843 the army and a crowd gathered here and refused to disperse until Otto granted a constitution; the square has been called Syntagma — Greek for constitution — ever since. The palace has housed the Parliament since 1934, and the monarchy it was built for was abolished by referendum in 1974. In 2010 to 2012 these same steps filled with protesters against the austerity that followed the debt crisis. Same stone, different century, same argument about who decides.

The square itself is free and open at all hours, with a metro station underneath and cafés all round it. Then walk east, past the fountain and across Amalias Avenue, to the gate of the National Garden.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. It is a public square and a memorial, not a ticketed site. The guard change costs nothing to watch.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Changing of the Guard every hour on the hour, on the hour; the Grand Change, with the full guard and a military band, is at 11:00 on Sunday mornings.
stops.accessibility: Level, paved square with wide pavements and step-free crossings. The forecourt of the tomb is flat but crowded at the change, and standing room fills up early on Sundays.
stops.insiderTip: Time it for the hour and stand to the side rather than straight in front of the guards. Sunday's 11:00 Grand Change brings the whole guard and the band — the best version, and the one locals turn out for.
stops.nextStopDirections: Cross Amalias Avenue at the lights on the square's east side and go through the gate into the National Garden. Walk south through the trees, past the duck and turtle ponds, and follow the paths down toward the big neoclassical hall at the garden's southern end — the Zappeion.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Jebulon, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: National Garden & Zappeion
stops.narration:
You are in fifteen hectares of shade, which in an Athens September is a small miracle. The National Garden was laid out in 1838 as the private Royal Garden of Queen Amalia, the young Bavarian wife of King Otto, and designed by a German agronomist who planted more than five hundred species — many of which died in the dry Attic heat before the survivors took hold. It stayed the royal family's back garden until 1924, and only became the 'National' Garden after the monarchy fell in the 1970s. It is free, open from dawn to dusk, and full of Athenians doing what Athenians do: walking, arguing, feeding the ducks and turtles, and letting children run.

Look for the older layer under the trees. The garden sits on Roman ruins — column drums, capitals and the floor mosaic of a Roman villa — and its south side carries busts of the men who made modern Greece, including Ioannis Kapodistrias, the first head of state of independent Greece, assassinated in 1831, and Dionysios Solomos, who wrote the poem that became the national anthem. At the southern edge stands the Zappeion, a neoclassical hall of 1888 by the Danish architect Theophil Hansen, paid for by Evangelis Zappas, a Greek benefactor who made a fortune in Romania and spent it reviving the ancient Olympic idea. Zappas died before the building opened; his embalmed head is walled up inside it, which is either macabre or magnificent depending on your taste. The Zappeion was the fencing hall of the first modern Olympics in 1896, later an Olympic village, and in 1979 the treaty taking Greece into what is now the European Union was signed in its atrium.

One dark story belongs here. In 1920 King Alexander was walking in this garden when he was bitten by a pet monkey; he died of infection three weeks later. His death brought back his deposed father, split the government, and helped set in motion the war with Turkey that ended in 1922 with the destruction of Smyrna and the expulsion of more than a million Greeks from Asia Minor. Winston Churchill remarked that 'a quarter of a million persons died of this monkey's bite.' The garden remembers none of it, and is all the better for that.

The Zappeion's interior opens only for exhibitions and events; the park around it is free. Exit at the southern gate by the Zappeion, onto Vasilissis Olgas Avenue, then walk north-west with the Parliament on your right.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. The garden is a public park; the Zappeion building itself opens only for exhibitions and events, which may charge admission.
stops.openingHours: Garden open daily from dawn to dusk. The Zappeion interior opens only during exhibitions and events — check locally.
stops.accessibility: The main paths are wide, level and step-free. Some side paths and the ground around the ponds are uneven and have steps, and the garden slopes gently uphill toward the Parliament.
stops.insiderTip: The tortoises and turtles around the ponds are residents, not decoration — watch your step. And look for the Roman mosaic floor and the scattered column drums among the trees; most people walk straight past them.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the garden at its southern gate by the Zappeion and walk north-west along Vasilissis Olgas Avenue, then up Amalias Avenue past the Parliament and Syntagma Square. Turn left into Mitropoleos Street and follow it south-west for about four hundred metres; the cathedral, with its twin bell towers and red-and-gold facade, is on your left.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Jakub Hałun, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Metropolitan Cathedral
stops.narration:
Two bell towers, a red-and-gold facade, and a queue of Athenians kissing the icon at the door: this is the Metropolitan Cathedral of the Annunciation, the mother church of the Church of Greece — 'Metropolis' to everyone who lives here. It was begun on Christmas Day 1842, when King Otto and Queen Amalia laid the cornerstone, and finished twenty years later. The architects kept changing and so did the plans; what you see is a three-aisled domed basilica, and its walls are made of marble stripped from seventy-two smaller churches demolished to build it. New nation, old stones.

Before you go in, look at the two statues on the square. One is Constantine XI Palaiologos, the last emperor of Byzantium, who died defending Constantinople in 1453 — the figure Greeks call the marble emperor, the one they believed would wake and retake the city. The other is Archbishop Damaskinos, who led the Church through the Nazi occupation, spoke out against the deportation of Greek Jews, and served as regent in the chaos after liberation. Church and nation, in two statues.

Step inside if the doors are open — quietly. This is a working church, not a monument: no ticket, no turnstile. Greek Orthodox churches are built around the liturgy rather than the sermon, and the walls are covered in icons — images of Christ, of Mary (the Theotokos, literally 'God-bearer') and of the saints, painted in the flat, golden style the tradition requires. Worshippers stand, cross themselves, and venerate icons by kissing them; women often cover their heads, and everyone dresses modestly. Photographs of the interior are usually fine when no service is running, but never photograph people at prayer. Under the floor lie the relics of two martyrs: Saint Philothei, killed in 1589 for ransoming Christian women from Ottoman households, and Patriarch Gregory V, hanged by the Sultan in 1821 in reprisal for the Greek uprising — the man whose death helped turn a revolt into a war.

The role of this church is bigger than religion. Under Ottoman rule the Orthodox patriarch was the empire's recognised leader of its Greek subjects, so the Church became the keeper of language, identity and memory. Independent Greece kept the tie: the Church of Greece has been autocephalous — self-governing — since 1833, and church and state are still not formally separated; priests are paid by the state and Orthodoxy is taught in schools. That closeness is debated. When the Church opposed the removal of religion from identity cards in 2000, or the legalisation of same-sex marriage in 2024, it spoke as a national institution, and plenty of Greeks disagreed with it. You are standing at the fault line.

Admission is free, and the cathedral is generally open from morning to early evening, closing to visitors during services. Then walk south-west along Mitropoleos Street, and turn left into the lanes of Plaka.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. It is a working cathedral, not a ticketed site. Donations are welcome but never required.
stops.openingHours: Generally open daily from early morning to early evening; free. Closed to visitors during services, especially on Sunday mornings and feast days — check at the door.
stops.accessibility: Level approach and a few shallow steps at the entrance. The floor inside is polished marble and level, but some chapels and the area around the relics have steps.
stops.insiderTip: Look at the two statues on the square before you go in — Constantine XI and Archbishop Damaskinos. Then find the Little Metropolis, the tiny twelfth-century church a few steps south, built almost entirely out of recycled ancient marble.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the cathedral walk south-west down Mitropoleos Street, then turn left into Apollonos Street and follow the pedestrian lanes into Plaka. In about three hundred metres you reach Adrianou Street, the old spine of the neighbourhood.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Dimitris Kamaras, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Plaka & Adrianou Street
stops.narration:
Adrianou Street is the oldest street you will walk today. It follows a line laid down in antiquity, was the first street in modern Athens to be paved — in 1835, when the new capital was still mostly rubble — and it splits Plaka in two: Ano Plaka, the upper quarter under the Acropolis, and Kato Plaka, the lower one toward Syntagma. Stand here and look both ways. Under the souvenir shops and tavernas is a neighbourhood inhabited continuously since the Neolithic, which is why archaeologists both love and curse it: every foundation dug for a bar hits something ancient.

The name Plaka is old and slightly mysterious. It appears in writing only in the 1600s, and it probably comes from the Arvanitika word plak, 'old' — Old Athens, in other words — though some argue it was a marble plaque at a crossroads. Either way, it was once a much smaller place than it sounds. Under Ottoman rule Athens was a provincial town of a few thousand people clustered on this slope; after independence in the 1830s the new capital was rebuilt on the grand neoclassical plan you can still see in the streets around Syntagma. Plaka was left as the old town, and was nearly lost in the 1960s to redevelopment before a preservation plan in the 1980s saved the lanes you are standing in. All the cables and pipes here run underground, by law, because Plaka is protected.

Read the street as a layer cake. The low whitewashed houses and walled gardens are mostly nineteenth-century; the small Byzantine churches tucked between them, like the eleventh-century Agios Nikolaos Ragavas, are a thousand years older. The tall neoclassical facades on the lower streets were the mansions of the first independent Greek state. And the quarter has taken in wave after wave of newcomers — Arvanites, the Albanian-speaking Orthodox Christians long settled in Greece; islanders; refugees from Asia Minor after 1922 — which is why it feels lived-in rather than preserved. People still live above these shops; the shutters open at eight in the morning and the rubbish goes out at night.

Eat and drink one street back from Adrianou if you can: the prices drop and the food usually improves. Nothing on the street is ticketed. The small Museum of Greek Popular Musical Instruments, just off the street, is cheap and worth a look — check its hours, as Greek museums keep short days. Then walk west and south, toward the white village stacked against the rock above you: Anafiotika.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. The street and lanes cost nothing; shops, tavernas and small museums charge their own prices, and the musical-instruments museum is inexpensive.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. The lanes and shops are liveliest from mid-morning to late evening; churches keep their own hours and close during services.
stops.accessibility: Mostly level and pedestrianised, but the paving is uneven stone with kerbs, occasional steps and gentle slopes off the main street. Anafiotika, above, is steep and stepped.
stops.insiderTip: Step one street back from Adrianou for cheaper food and fewer souvenir shops, and hunt for the small Byzantine churches wedged between the houses — Agios Nikolaos Ragavas, a few steps off the street, is eleventh-century and easy to walk past.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk west and then south up the stepped lanes past the little church of Agios Nikolaos Ragavas, following the signs for Anafiotika. The street narrows, the houses turn white, and after a few hundred metres of climbing you are in the village.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: George E. Koronaios, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Anafiotika
stops.narration:
You have climbed into a village that should not be here. Anafiotika is a cluster of about forty-five whitewashed, flat-roofed houses on the north-east slope of the Acropolis, built in the style of the Cyclades — the Aegean island group — with blue shutters, tiny courtyards and bougainvillea spilling over the walls. There is no grid, no square, and most of the lanes have no names at all: the houses are simply numbered, Anafiotika 1, Anafiotika 2. If it feels like an island, that is exactly the point.

It was built in the 1830s and 1840s by workmen from Anafi, a small Cycladic island east of Santorini whose population is a few hundred even today. They came to Athens to build and refurbish King Otto's new palace, and like builders everywhere they needed somewhere to live; they settled on the slope below the Acropolis, where the land was nobody's, and built the houses they knew how to build. The first two recorded residents were a carpenter and a construction worker. More islanders followed — masons, carpenters, marble-cutters — and the settlement grew. After 1922 it took in refugees from Asia Minor, and for a century it was a poor, half-hidden quarter that the rest of Athens mostly ignored.

That invisibility saved it, and then nearly destroyed it. In 1950 part of the neighbourhood was demolished for archaeological excavation, and from the 1970s the state began buying the houses, one by one, to clear the slope. Residents fought back, and what survived is what you see: a fragment, roughly half the original village, now protected and fiercely expensive. Walk slowly and look at the details — the tiny church of Agios Georgios tou Vrachou, Saint George of the Rock, built into the cliff at the top of the lane, and the wall of the Acropolis rising directly above the rooftops.

A word about manners, because people live in every one of these houses. This is not a museum village: there are laundry lines, cats, old men on chairs and children's bicycles. Keep your voice down, do not photograph through open doors or into courtyards, and do not climb on walls or into gardens for a view — the residents have had enough of that. The best view is from the top of the lane anyway, where the white roofs fall away toward the city and the sea beyond.

There is nothing to pay here and little to buy beyond the odd café; it is a neighbourhood, not a site. Then walk back down, west and north, toward the ruins and the octagonal marble tower below — the Roman Agora.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. It is a lived-in neighbourhood, not a ticketed site — there is nothing to pay and no gate to pass.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times, but this is a residential quarter: visit by day, keep quiet, and do not enter private courtyards or gardens.
stops.accessibility: Not accessible, honestly: steep, narrow, stepped lanes with uneven surfaces and no handrails. The climb is short but real, and there is no step-free route through.
stops.insiderTip: Find the little church of Agios Georgios tou Vrachou, built into the rock at the top of the lane — and remember that every house here is someone's home. Photograph the lanes and rooftops, not the doorways.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk back down the lanes to the north-west, following the slope toward the octagonal marble tower you can see below. In about four hundred metres the lanes open into the Roman Agora, at the bottom of the hill.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Ranssom, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Roman Agora & Tower of the Winds
stops.narration:
Under your feet is Athens' Roman shopping centre. When the Romans took Greece, the old Agora to the west became a religious and civic square, so in about 10 BC the city built a new market here, paid for with money from the emperor Augustus in fulfilment of a promise Julius Caesar had made fifty years earlier. You are standing at its western gate, the Gate of Athena Archegetis — Athena the Leader, the city's patron — a marble doorway whose inscription records a decree of Hadrian's reign about the tax obligations of oil merchants. That is the Roman Agora in one detail: colonnades, shops, a fountain, public latrines, and an office for market inspectors. A mall with a customs desk.

But the reason to pay the ticket is the octagonal tower in the middle: the Tower of the Winds, the Horologion of Andronikos of Cyrrhus, built around 50 BC and the only surviving ancient clock tower in the world. It is Pentelic marble, twelve metres tall and eight across, with eight sides and a different wind god carved on each: Boreas the cold north wind in winter clothes, Kaikias the north-east emptying a shield of hail, Apeliotes the east carrying fruit, Notus the south tipping a water jar to promise rain, and so on. Above the figures ran a bronze weather vane in the shape of Triton, pointing to whichever wind was blowing; below, on the walls, are the lines of eight sundials, each cut for the hours that face actually caught the sun. Inside was a water clock, fed by a spring on the Acropolis above through a channel in the floor, whose holes and grooves you can still see. The shadow-casting pins, the gnomons, were long ago stolen; the holes that held them remain, and modern replacements have been fitted.

The tower has had more lives than most people get. It was probably a church or baptistry in late antiquity — there is a cross cut into one inner wall. By Ottoman times it was buried up to half its height, with houses built against it, and from 1751 to 1821 it served as a tekke, a lodge where Qadiri dervishes — Muslim mystics — performed their rituals, cutting a prayer niche into the wall. When British architects measured it in the 1750s, it became one of the first ancient Greek buildings published in western Europe, and it helped set off the whole neoclassical fashion.

Tickets are around €10, with a reduced rate, and there is no combined ticket any more — each site is priced separately, so verify the price and the hours at the gate, as both change. Expect roughly 08:00 to 20:00 in high season and shorter winter days. The ticket office is around the corner on Epaminonda Street, not at the gate itself. The ground is ancient paving: uneven, with steps and no railings, so watch your feet. Then walk north-west, past the ruins of Hadrian's Library, toward the square where the city's bazaar begins.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Around €10, reduced about €5. Since 2025 each archaeological site is ticketed separately — there is no combined Acropolis ticket — so verify the price at the gate. The ticket office is around the corner on Epaminonda Street, not at the entrance.
stops.openingHours: Hours vary sharply by season: often roughly 08:00 to 20:00 in high summer, and as short as about 08:30 to 16:00 out of season, with last entry usually thirty minutes before closing. Confirm on the day — do not rely on a fixed time.
stops.accessibility: Uneven ancient paving, worn steps and no handrails; the tower itself has no ramp. The main paths are walkable but not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Find the wind gods' names carved above each figure, then look for the sundial lines and the modern gnomons on the sun-facing walls. And check where you buy the ticket — it is around the corner on Epaminonda Street, not at the gate.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave by the western gate and walk about three hundred metres north-west along the pedestrian street, past the tall columns and the fenced ruins of Hadrian's Library on your left. The lanes open into Monastiraki Square, with the metro entrance and the mosque in front of you.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Jakub Hałun, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Monastiraki Square & the Flea Market
stops.narration:
Monastiraki means 'little monastery', and the name comes from the church in the middle of this square: the Pantanassa, a tenth-century church that was once the main building of a monastery known as the Great Monastery, until the monastery vanished and only the 'little' one was left. Around it grew the bazaar that made this the busiest corner of Ottoman Athens — and the name stuck to the whole neighbourhood. It is a fitting end to the walk, because Monastiraki is where old Athens, immigrant Athens and tourist Athens all collide in one square.

Two buildings tell the story. The first is the Tzistarakis Mosque, built in 1759 by the Ottoman governor of Athens. Legend says he made the lime for its walls by breaking up a column from the Temple of Olympian Zeus, and that a plague and his own disgrace followed — the city took its ancient monuments seriously even then. It is a mosque no longer: it has been a prison, a barracks and a storeroom, and it is now an annex of the Museum of Greek Folk Art. The second is the metro station beside it, on Line 1 — the oldest railway line in Greece, opened in 1869 as the Athens to Piraeus railway, when this was the edge of town and the trains ran on steam.

Now walk the market. The sign at the top of Ifestou Street announces 'the Flea Market of Athens', and the street below is lined with second-hand shops, old records, posters and junk. The real flea market, though, is on Sunday mornings in Avissinia Square at the western end of Ifestou: tables of antiques, coins, tools and pure rubbish, with the Acropolis looking down on all of it. On any other day the trade is mostly souvenirs and cheap clothes, so buy for fun rather than investment — and remember that taking genuine antiquities out of Greece is illegal.

Before you leave, look north-west up the street to the ruins of Hadrian's Library. The emperor Hadrian built it in AD 132 as a vast colonnaded complex with a hundred columns of coloured marble, a courtyard, a pool and lecture halls; it was wrecked by invaders in AD 267 and patched up, then became a churchyard — the first cathedral of Athens, the Megali Panagia, stood inside it in the twelfth century. It is a separate ticket now, around €10, so verify at the gate if you want to go in.

The square and the market are free and open all day, liveliest in the evening and on Sunday mornings, and the metro will take you anywhere from here. Two hundred metres north, the bars of Psyrri fill with people after dark, and the souvlaki shops along Mitropoleos — Thanasis, Savvas and Bairaktaris — have been arguing about who is best for generations. This is where the tour ends, but it is also where Athens begins its evening: sit down, order something, and watch the square fill up. You have walked from a king's constitution to a sultan's mosque and back, through a couple of kilometres of the oldest streets in Europe.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. The square and market streets cost nothing; individual shops, the mosque-museum annex and food are priced separately.
stops.openingHours: Square and market open all day; the shops along Ifestou Street keep normal trading hours, and the real flea market runs on Sunday mornings in Avissinia Square. The mosque-museum keeps museum hours.
stops.accessibility: Level, paved square with kerbs and metro paving; step-free around the square itself. The market streets are flat but crowded and uneven underfoot.
stops.insiderTip: Come back on a Sunday morning for the real flea market in Avissinia Square, at the west end of Ifestou Street — and look up from the stalls to the Acropolis above the rooftops.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Monastiraki metro station is right here, on Lines 1 and 3, so the rest of the city is minutes away; if you would rather keep going, walk two hundred metres north into Psyrri for the bars, or follow Mitropoleos back for souvlaki. Take your time — this is the hour the square is at its best.
